passages.title: Solomon seeks wisdom
passages.summary: Solomon seeks wisdom at Gibeon. The chapter also describes royal wealth, horses, and trade.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Markers do not establish exact ancient roads or political boundaries.

lds.text: Why does Solomon ask for wisdom before asking for wealth?

contextNote.title: The opening connects rule with a need for judgment
contextNote.text: Solomon asks for wisdom to govern people rather than simply acquire goods. The following wealth description stands beside that request. Readers can assess abundance through the responsibility named first.

passages.title: Temple workers and Tyrian cooperation
passages.summary: Solomon requests timber and skilled work from Huram. Foreign residents supply the labor force.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Markers do not establish exact ancient roads or political boundaries.

lds.text: Whose skills and labor make the temple possible?

contextNote.title: A sacred building depends on workers outside the ruling household
contextNote.text: Solomon counts foreign residents and assigns them carrying, cutting, and supervision. Huram also supplies specialized skill. The temple account includes imposed labor as well as international cooperation.

passages.title: The temple building
passages.summary: Solomon builds the temple at the site associated with David and Ornan. Rooms, decoration, and pillars receive detailed descriptions.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Markers do not establish exact ancient roads or political boundaries.

lds.text: The Seminary manual connects Moriah with sacred space and temple worship.

contextNote.title: The site connects the new building with an earlier crisis
contextNote.text: The temple stands where David prepared an altar after the plague. Its location therefore carries memory beyond architectural beauty. Solomon's work develops a place already marked by judgment and response.

passages.title: Temple vessels and bronze work
passages.summary: Huram makes bronze vessels. Solomon provides the temple’s gold objects and furnishings.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Markers do not establish exact ancient roads or political boundaries.

lds.text: What different tasks do the temple’s vessels serve?

contextNote.title: Water and metal serve different tasks
contextNote.text: The account distinguishes water for priests from water for washing offerings. The crafted basins serve repeated work around the temple. Their size and placement make worship depend on planned spaces. Read the objects through their tasks, not only their beauty. Regional metalwork offers comparison without reconstructing these exact vessels.

passages.title: The ark enters the temple
passages.summary: Priests bring the ark into the inner sanctuary. Singers and trumpeters praise together, and a cloud fills the house.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Markers do not establish exact ancient roads or political boundaries.

lds.text: The Seminary manual compares dedication experiences with later LDS temple worship.

contextNote.title: Coordinated sound prepares the scene of shared worship
contextNote.text: Singers and trumpeters praise together rather than as separate displays. The cloud then prevents priests from continuing their normal service. Ordered human work leads into an encounter they cannot direct.

passages.title: Solomon’s dedication prayer
passages.summary: Solomon blesses the assembly and prays for justice, forgiveness, foreigners, and people taken captive.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Markers do not establish exact ancient roads or political boundaries.

lds.text: Why does Solomon include foreigners in his prayer?

contextNote.title: The dedication includes people outside the covenant community
contextNote.text: Solomon asks that a foreigner's prayer be heard. He also imagines people praying from captivity. The temple's role reaches beyond those present at its first celebration.

passages.title: Dedication and a conditional promise
passages.summary: The assembly celebrates the dedication. God’s response calls for humility and repentance and warns against abandoned commitments.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Markers do not establish exact ancient roads or political boundaries.

lds.text: The Seminary manual studies the dedication as an account of divine acceptance.

contextNote.title: The promise leaves open the possibility of rejection
contextNote.text: God's response includes both restored hearing and future loss. The celebrated building can become a warning to others. Its physical presence does not guarantee that the community will remain faithful.

passages.title: Construction, labor, and sea trade
passages.summary: Solomon develops towns, assigns forced labor, organizes worship, and works with Huram’s sailors. Pharaoh’s daughter receives a separate residence.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Markers do not establish exact ancient roads or political boundaries.

lds.text: How do workers and sailors support Solomon’s kingdom?

contextNote.title: Building achievement requires repeated service afterward
contextNote.text: The account moves from construction into offerings and assigned divisions. Festivals and daily duties make the structures places of continuing use. Completion of buildings is only one stage of temple life.

passages.title: Sheba’s queen and Solomon’s reputation
passages.summary: The queen of Sheba tests Solomon with questions. Gifts and trade bring him wealth. Rehoboam becomes king after his death.

passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Markers do not establish exact ancient roads or political boundaries.

lds.text: What does the queen ask about Solomon’s wisdom and God’s care for Israel?

contextNote.title: Admiration describes the court from a visitor's position
contextNote.text: The queen praises the attendants who hear Solomon's wisdom. The account also names wealth and imported horses. The next chapter supplies the subjects' different perspective on the burden inherited from this reign.

passages.title: Rehoboam refuses relief
passages.summary: The people ask Rehoboam to reduce their burden. He chooses harsh advice, and the northern tribes reject his rule.

passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Markers do not establish exact ancient roads or political boundaries.

lds.text: Why does Rehoboam reject the advice to ease the people’s burden?

contextNote.title: Advice differs over how authority is secured
contextNote.text: The elders recommend kindness as a way to gain continued service. The younger advisers recommend a stronger threat. Rehoboam's choice treats relief as weakness and produces the division he feared.

passages.title: Defense, migration, and royal families
passages.summary: Shemaiah stops Rehoboam’s attack on the northern tribes. Rehoboam strengthens towns and welcomes priests and Levites. He also plans which son will rule.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Markers do not establish exact ancient roads or political boundaries.

lds.text: Why do priests and Levites leave the northern kingdom?

contextNote.title: A prophetic refusal limits the new king's military response
contextNote.text: Rehoboam gathers forces to recover the northern tribes. Shemaiah's message stops the campaign against their relatives. The remaining preparations turn toward defense rather than forced reunion.

passages.title: Shishak and a reduced kingdom
passages.summary: Shishak takes Judah's defended towns and Jerusalem's treasures. Rehoboam humbles himself but later leaves God.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Markers do not establish exact ancient roads or political boundaries.

lds.text: How does Rehoboam respond when Shemaiah explains Judah’s defeat?

contextNote.title: Reduced independence receives an explicit explanation
contextNote.text: The people will serve Shishak instead of retaining full freedom. The message presents this as learning the difference between forms of service. Lost treasure makes the change in power visible.

passages.title: Abijah’s speech and war
passages.summary: Abijah appeals to David’s covenant and temple worship while confronting Jeroboam. Judah wins the battle.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Markers do not establish exact ancient roads or political boundaries.

lds.text: What reasons does Abijah give for Judah’s trust in God?

contextNote.title: A battle speech argues through the institutions of worship
contextNote.text: Abijah contrasts Judah's priests and temple service with Jeroboam's arrangements. His speech frames the conflict through competing religious claims. The account gives this argument a central place before describing victory.

passages.title: Asa changes worship and asks for help
passages.summary: Asa removes worship objects and strengthens towns. He calls for divine help against Zerah’s forces.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Markers do not establish exact ancient roads or political boundaries.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me invites study of Asa’s trust during danger.

contextNote.title: Preparation and petition share the account of defense
contextNote.text: Asa strengthens towns during rest and asks for help during invasion. His prayer does not erase the earlier practical work. The chapter places both efforts within its explanation of survival.

passages.title: Azariah’s warning and covenant
passages.summary: Azariah addresses Asa. The assembly renews its covenant, and Asa removes Maacah’s royal status.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Markers do not establish exact ancient roads or political boundaries.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies perseverance and trust through Asa’s reforms.

contextNote.title: A spoken warning becomes a public commitment
contextNote.text: Azariah's message prompts repair and a gathered covenant. The renewed agreement includes people who came from northern tribes. Religious boundaries and political boundaries do not perfectly coincide.

passages.title: Asa’s alliance and anger
passages.summary: Asa pays Ben Hadad to break his treaty with Baasha. Hanani rebukes Asa, who imprisons him and oppresses others.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Markers do not establish exact ancient roads or political boundaries.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me compares where Asa places his trust at different times.

contextNote.title: A ruler's response to criticism changes his judgment
contextNote.text: Asa gains military relief through the foreign agreement. Hanani challenges how he obtained it. Imprisonment and oppression then show the danger of protecting a decision from correction.

passages.title: Jehoshaphat teaches and strengthens Judah
passages.summary: Jehoshaphat sends teachers through Judah with God's law. He also builds defenses and gathers soldiers.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Markers do not establish exact ancient roads or political boundaries.

lds.text: How does Jehoshaphat use teachers to help his people learn God’s law?

contextNote.title: Instruction carries the law beyond the capital
contextNote.text: The teachers travel through the towns with the written law. Their work makes royal policy include shared learning. Soldiers and defenses are therefore not the chapter's only means of strengthening Judah.

passages.title: Micaiah and the war with Ahab
passages.summary: Jehoshaphat joins Ahab. Micaiah challenges favorable predictions and reports a heavenly council before Ahab dies in battle.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Markers do not establish exact ancient roads or political boundaries.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies Micaiah’s truthful speech under pressure.

contextNote.title: Approved predictions place pressure on an independent speaker
contextNote.text: The messenger asks Micaiah to agree with the others. Micaiah's answer separates speaking faithfully from pleasing the court. The account exposes a consultation that already has a preferred result.

passages.title: Correction and impartial judgment
passages.summary: Jehu rebukes Jehoshaphat’s alliance. The king appoints judges and distinguishes religious and royal responsibilities.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Markers do not establish exact ancient roads or political boundaries.

lds.text: The Seminary manual connects correction with faithful service.

contextNote.title: Judicial work requires limits on personal advantage
contextNote.text: Jehoshaphat warns judges against partiality and accepting gifts. Authority to decide disputes comes with duties toward those appearing before them. The king's reform addresses daily justice after correction of his own conduct.

passages.title: Prayer, Jahaziel, and deliverance
passages.summary: Jehoshaphat gathers the people for prayer. Jahaziel speaks encouragement. The opposing forces destroy one another, and Judah returns with plunder.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Markers do not establish exact ancient roads or political boundaries.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies prayer, trust, and prophetic encouragement.

contextNote.title: Public prayer names the limits of royal knowledge
contextNote.text: Jehoshaphat admits that the assembly does not know what to do. Jahaziel's reply gives direction within that shared uncertainty. The king's leadership begins with acknowledgment rather than a claim of complete control.

passages.title: Jehoram’s violence and decline
passages.summary: Jehoram kills his brothers and adopts Ahab’s family practices. Revolts, invasion, Elijah’s letter, and illness mark his reign.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Markers do not establish exact ancient roads or political boundaries.

lds.text: How do Jehoram’s choices affect his brothers and the people he rules?

contextNote.title: Securing a throne can destroy the household that supports it
contextNote.text: Jehoram kills his brothers after gaining power. Their gifts and positions do not protect them from his suspicion. The later decline makes this early violence part of the reign's moral account.

passages.title: Ahaziah dies and Joash is hidden
passages.summary: Ahaziah follows Ahab’s family and dies during Jehu’s overthrow. Jehoshabeath and a nurse protect Joash from Athaliah.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Markers do not establish exact ancient roads or political boundaries.

lds.text: What do Jehoshabeath and the nurse risk by hiding Joash?

contextNote.title: Protection makes a later coronation possible
contextNote.text: Jehoshabeath and the nurse hide Joash during the royal killings. Their care keeps the family line alive before any public recognition. The later coronation depends on years of work in concealment.

passages.title: Jehoiada installs Joash
passages.summary: Jehoiada organizes guards and worship workers. Joash receives the crown, Athaliah dies, and a covenant follows.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Markers do not establish exact ancient roads or political boundaries.

lds.text: Why does Jehoiada ask the people to promise loyalty to God when Joash becomes king?

contextNote.title: A coronation restores obligations as well as a ruler
contextNote.text: Jehoiada makes a covenant linking king and people with God. The subsequent changes organize temple access and service. The new reign begins through shared duties rather than a crown alone.

passages.title: Temple repair and Zechariah’s death
passages.summary: Joash repairs the temple during Jehoiada’s life. Afterward he rejects correction and orders Zechariah’s death. His own servants later kill him.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Markers do not establish exact ancient roads or political boundaries.

lds.text: Why does Joash reject correction after Jehoiada’s death?

contextNote.title: The king forgets the care that preserved his position
contextNote.text: Joash kills the son of Jehoiada after receiving that family's protection. Temple repair earlier marked his reign as restoration. The account contrasts preserving a building with refusing the correction spoken within it.

passages.title: Amaziah’s victories and defeat
passages.summary: Amaziah dismisses hired troops, defeats Edom, adopts its gods, and refuses a prophet. Joash of Israel defeats him.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Markers do not establish exact ancient roads or political boundaries.

lds.text: How does Amaziah respond differently to his two warnings?

contextNote.title: A successful king tries to silence the judgment of success
contextNote.text: Amaziah threatens the prophet who questions his adopted gods. His later challenge to Israel likewise rejects warning. Victory becomes dangerous when it makes correction seem unnecessary.

passages.title: Uzziah’s strength and forbidden incense
passages.summary: Uzziah builds towns, farms, and defenses. The priest Azariah stops his attempt to burn incense. Uzziah becomes ill.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Markers do not establish exact ancient roads or political boundaries.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies humility and the limits on Uzziah’s incense offering.

contextNote.title: Royal success does not confer every sacred role
contextNote.text: Uzziah's achievements precede his attempt to burn incense. The priests identify a duty reserved for another office. The account sets a boundary on the king's authority inside the temple.

passages.title: Jotham builds and governs
passages.summary: Jotham strengthens Jerusalem and other towns. Ammon pays him tribute. He follows God, but the people continue doing wrong.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Markers do not establish exact ancient roads or political boundaries.

lds.text: What can a faithful leader do when others continue doing wrong?

contextNote.title: A ruler's conduct does not automatically change the people
contextNote.text: Jotham receives praise while the people continue doing wrong. The account distinguishes the king's course from theirs. Public strength does not establish a shared moral outcome.

passages.title: Ahaz, captives, and Oded’s intervention
passages.summary: Ahaz suffers defeats and seeks Assyrian help. Oded and northern leaders secure humane care and return for Judah’s captives.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Markers do not establish exact ancient roads or political boundaries.

lds.text: How do the northern leaders turn a victory into care for their captives?

contextNote.title: A prophetic appeal changes the treatment of defeated enemies
contextNote.text: Oded warns Israel against enslaving captives from Judah. Northern leaders provide clothing, food, and transport instead. The episode interrupts a reign's violence with care across the divided kingdom.

passages.title: Hezekiah restores temple service
passages.summary: Hezekiah opens the temple and calls workers to cleanse it. Sacrifice and music resume with public thanksgiving.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Markers do not establish exact ancient roads or political boundaries.

lds.text: What work must the priests and Levites finish before temple worship can begin again?

contextNote.title: Restoration joins specialized duties with broad participation
contextNote.text: Priests and Levites perform different parts of the cleansing and offerings. The assembly also responds through worship and gifts. Renewed service requires organized work rather than the king's order alone.

passages.title: Passover invitations and pardon
passages.summary: Hezekiah invites northern communities to Jerusalem. Some mock the couriers, but others attend. He prays for participants who lack ritual preparation.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · reign and composition dates require comparison
passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Markers do not establish exact ancient roads or political boundaries.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies welcome, pardon, and peacemaking at Passover.

contextNote.title: The invitation reaches beyond perfect ritual preparation

guides.title: 2 Chronicles: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: Water and metal serve different tasks
steps.text: The account distinguishes water for priests from water for washing offerings. The crafted basins serve repeated work around the temple. Their size and placement make worship depend on planned spaces. Read the objects through their tasks, not only their beauty. Regional metalwork offers comparison without reconstructing these exact vessels.

steps.title: Defense combines work and trust
steps.text: Hezekiah repairs walls and prepares weapons while facing Assyria. His speech asks the people to trust God. The account presents practical defense and prayer together. Assyrian records describe the campaign from the attacking king’s side. Compare the accounts without treating royal claims as neutral reports.

steps.title: The last royal speech opens a road beyond exile
steps.text: The final speech comes from Cyrus, a foreign ruler. It allows a return and the rebuilding of a temple. The book ends with movement ahead rather than another Judahite king. The Cyrus Cylinder gives wider context for Persian restoration claims. It does not name this return or prove every detail of the speech.
